question: Why does direct supervision beat recursive critique when a stronger model supervises a weaker one, and would better critique abilities change that?
asked_by: Wen et al., Scalable Oversight for Superhuman AI via Recursive Self-Critiquing
remaining_question: In AI-AI recursive self-critiquing where the critic is stronger than the supervised model, does improving the supervised model's self-critique (for example by RL critique training) or making the critic verify rather than defer to that self-critique remove the advantage of direct critique over higher-order critique on the asking paper's tasks?

blockers.name: A measurement
blockers.next: On the asking paper's tasks, improve the supervised model's self-critique (for example by RL critique training) or make the stronger critic verify rather than defer to it, and test whether direct critique still beats higher-order critique.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2605.27483v1: Debate Helps Weak Judges Reward Stronger Models
findings.claim: In proposer-critic debate with a stronger debater and a weaker judge, debate raised macro-F1 over consultancy on three of five model pairings and had no effect on two; the authors report that the split follows whether the critic's classifier macro-F1 exceeds the judge's and whether the judge verifies rather than summarises the critic's claims, with verification rates dropping by tens of points once a critic entered on the non-responder pairings. They flag this as a hypothesis well supported within five pairings, not a law.
findings.setting: Empirical. Five stronger-debater/weaker-judge LLM pairings: Qwen3.5-122B/35B, gpt-oss-120B/20B and Qwen3.5-35B/Qwen3-4B on Code Contests, Gemini 3.1 Pro/3 Flash and Opus 4.6/4.5 on ARC-AGI-2; programmatically verifiable tasks; LLM judges; consultancy baseline. No recursive critique and no strong-critic/weak-supervised setting.
findings.bears_on: By analogy only, the 'would better critique abilities change it' part: a critique helps its reader only when the critic out-classifies the reader and the reader verifies it. Not tested for higher-order self-critique by a weaker supervised model read by a stronger critic.

passages.text:
ground truth—proposer–critic debate raises macro-F1 over consultancy on three of five model pairings
and shows no effect on the other two. The split is governed by a single condition: debate helps only
when the critic provides a usable advantage. That condition has two sub-parts, both of which must
hold. First, the critic’s classifier macro-F1 must exceed the opening-only consultancy judge’s—there
has to be a margin worth importing; raw judge capability and the critic’s generator–verifier gap
do not predict the split, but this critic–judge classifier gap does. Second, the judge must treat the
critic’s stance as a claim to verify rather than testimony to summarize. Behavior reviews of the
transcripts (§4.2, Appendix L) show the mechanism: on responder pairings both sub-parts hold and
judges import the critic’s signal; on the two non-responder pairings in our set, both sub-parts fail
together—the critic’s and judge’s binary-classification ability are within noise of each other, and
verification rates drop by tens of percentage points once a critic enters the transcript, with the critic’s
disagreement parsed as testimony rather than a claim to check.

We flag a small-N caveat: with five pairings, the gap diagnostic is a hypothesis well-supported
within our experimental set, not a law established at scale. We also note that with ARC-AGI-2
substantially harder than Code Contests, our pairings do not let us cleanly separate the critic–judge
gap from broader capability differences; the two conditions we identify (judge verification behavior
and critic–judge classifier gap) are themselves capability properties, just more specific ones than
raw solve rate. Whether the same mechanism transfers to fuzzier domains where programmatic
verification is unavailable is a hypothesis warranting further work, not a finding from our experiments.

Debate improves macro-F1 over consultancy on three of five pairings and has no effect on the other
two (Figure 2). It helps Qwen3.5-122B/35B on Code Contests (+14.0pp under our canonical prompt
and +7.3pp under a simpler one, both p < 0.001), and Gemini 3.1 Pro/3 Flash and Opus 4.6/4.5
on ARC-AGI-2 (+14.0pp and +15.7pp, both p < 0.01). It does not help gpt-oss-120B/20B or
Qwen3.5-35B/Qwen3-4B on Code Contests (+1.4pp, p = 0.23 and −0.2pp, p = 0.93). We call the
first group responder pairings and the second non-responder pairings.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2606.00424v2: Weak Critics Make Strong Learners: On-Policy Critique Distillation for Scalable Oversight
findings.claim: With a weak model critiquing a stronger model's answer before the strong model revises, the authors report that weak critiques improved the frozen strong model, but that misleading critiques can hurt performance even relative to no critique; reusing a critique from a chain where a correct answer was revised to an incorrect one ('worst critic') performed worst among the critique-quality baselines on GPQA Diamond, falling slightly below the strong model alone (S) only at pass@16.
findings.setting: Empirical, inference-time critique-and-refine (the paper's training method is not quoted here). A weak critic (W) critiques a frozen strong model's (S) initial answer, which the strong model then revises; Phi-4 results on GPQA Diamond, with IFEval also reported; pass@k. The best/worst-critic baselines are chosen post hoc from outcome labels. Not recursive critique read by a stronger critic.
findings.bears_on: Related evidence that critiques from a weaker model can mislead a stronger model and that critique quality matters, but in a weak-critic/strong-reviser setting, not recursive self-critique judged by a stronger critic.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2509.05396v2: Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Understanding Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
findings.claim: In multi-agent debate among LLM agents of differing capability, the authors report that introducing a weaker agent into a debate with a stronger one can detrimentally affect the outcome, giving results worse than if the agents had not discussed, and that the weaker agent disrupts the stronger agent's performance. Separately, among agents that change their answers, more shift from correct to incorrect than the reverse, which the authors say indicates that debate can actively mislead agents who started with correct answers.
findings.setting: Empirical. Multi-round multi-agent debate among LLM agents, including debates that mix a weaker and a stronger agent; answer transitions between correct and incorrect tracked across rounds; not recursive critique by a stronger supervisor.
findings.bears_on: Corroborates, in a different protocol, the asking paper's explanation that a weaker model's reasoning can mislead a stronger one; says nothing about whether better critique ability would change the result.
